reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / WHO / India national programmes
clinicalPearls: Central nervous system infection by larval Taenia solium and one of the leading causes of acquired epilepsy in India and other endemic regions
Seizures are the most frequent presentation, typically from a single or few degenerating parenchymal cysts
Clinical features depend on cyst number, location and stage, ranging from asymptomatic calcified lesions to disabling neurological disease
Extraparenchymal disease (intraventricular, subarachnoid or racemose forms) can obstruct cerebrospinal fluid flow and cause hydrocephalus, and behaves more aggressively
MRI and CT are central to diagnosis; the finding of a cyst with a visible scolex is highly characteristic, and calcified lesions indicate old, dead cysts
Antiparasitic therapy is combined with corticosteroids to blunt the inflammatory reaction to dying cysts, with antiseizure medication for those presenting with seizures
Treatment must be individualised: viable parenchymal cysts, calcified lesions and intraventricular cysts are managed differently, and some forms need neurosurgical intervention
Fundoscopy or ophthalmic assessment is advised before antiparasitic treatment to exclude ocular cysts
reference.pathophysiology: Ingested Taenia solium eggs release oncospheres that reach the brain and develop into cysticerci. Viable cysts in the parenchyma may remain quiescent, but immune-mediated degeneration releases antigens that provoke perilesional inflammation and oedema, generating seizures and focal deficits. As cysts die they may calcify, and these calcified foci can remain epileptogenic. In the ventricles and subarachnoid space, cysts and the associated inflammation can block cerebrospinal fluid pathways, producing raised intracranial pressure and hydrocephalus, while subarachnoid (racemose) disease may cause arachnoiditis and vasculitis.
additionalDifferentials: Other parasitic CNS lesions (e.g. hydatid cyst)
additionalInvestigations: MRI brain to characterise cyst stage, detect a scolex and assess perilesional oedema
Serological antibody testing (e.g. EITB) as supportive evidence
Ophthalmological examination to exclude ocular cysts before therapy
CSF studies and assessment for hydrocephalus in suspected extraparenchymal disease
redFlags: New-onset or breakthrough seizures, including status epilepticus, requiring urgent management
Signs of raised intracranial pressure or hydrocephalus from intraventricular disease, a neurosurgical emergency
Rapid neurological deterioration precipitated by inflammation when antiparasitic therapy is started
Focal deficits, altered consciousness or signs of stroke from subarachnoid vasculitis
reference.prognosis: Solitary parenchymal cysts often resolve with good seizure control and a favourable outcome, though some patients develop chronic epilepsy from residual calcified lesions. Extraparenchymal, subarachnoid and heavy-burden disease carries a worse prognosis with risk of hydrocephalus, recurrent complications and higher mortality.
pitfalls: Giving antiparasitic drugs without corticosteroid cover, risking severe inflammatory worsening and seizures
Treating without first excluding ocular or intraventricular cysts, where drug-induced inflammation is dangerous
Assuming all ring-enhancing brain lesions are neurocysticercosis and missing tuberculoma or tumour
Overlooking hydrocephalus as a cause of deterioration in extraparenchymal disease
management: Give antiparasitic therapy with albendazole, with or without praziquantel, to hasten resolution of viable parenchymal cysts
Co-administer corticosteroids with antiparasitic treatment to blunt the inflammatory reaction to dying cysts and control perilesional oedema
Control seizures with antiseizure medication, a mainstay for those presenting with epilepsy
Exclude ocular cysticercosis by ophthalmological examination before starting antiparasitic therapy to avoid sight-threatening inflammation

Manage extraparenchymal disease and hydrocephalus with neurosurgical intervention such as endoscopic cyst removal or cerebrospinal fluid diversion, often with prolonged antiparasitic and corticosteroid therapy
Withhold antiparasitic drugs in calcified-only (dead) lesions and in cysticercal encephalitis with diffuse oedema, treating supportively
Institute public health measures and family screening for taeniasis, with follow-up imaging to confirm lesion resolution

valueTables.title: Diagnostic criteria for human cysticercosis

cells.text: Cysticerci shown on histologic or microscopic examination of biopsy material; parasite seen in the eye on funduscopy; neuroradiologic demonstration of cystic lesions containing a characteristic scolex

Neuroradiologic lesions suggestive of neurocysticercosis; antibodies to cysticerci in serum by enzyme-linked immunoelectrotransfer blot; spontaneous resolution of intracranial cystic lesions, or resolution after albendazole or praziquantel alone

Lesions compatible with neurocysticercosis on neuroimaging; clinical manifestations suggestive of neurocysticercosis; antibodies to cysticerci or cysticercal antigen in cerebrospinal fluid by ELISA; cysticercosis outside the CNS (for example cigar-shaped soft-tissue calcifications)
Residence in a cysticercosis-endemic area; frequent travel to an endemic area; household contact with a person infected with Taenia solium
